title: How to repurpose long-form content into social posts on Mac: a routine for marketers
metaTitle: How to repurpose long-form content into social posts on Mac
description: Turn one long article into a week of social posts on Mac. Costs, causes, a repeatable routine, and fixes you can use today, plus where Lazur helps.
targetKeyword: how to repurpose long-form content into social posts
secondaryKeywords: turn a blog post into social posts
social media posts from one article
intro: To repurpose long-form content into social posts, pull one idea per post, rewrite each idea for the platform it goes to, and schedule the set before you start the next piece. Start with an article you already published, not a blank page. This guide covers the cost, the causes, fixes you can use without buying anything, and where Lazur fits in.
tldr: Plan the posts before you write the long piece. Repurposing done after publishing is the version that stalls.
Each platform needs its own version. Copying one post everywhere is crossposting, not repurposing.
Sprout Social reports about 5 hours a week on content creation and approvals for full-time social marketers.
Fixes that use apps you likely have: a post map in Google Docs, a status sheet in Google Sheets, a batch review in Slack.
Lazur can explain, point, guide and draft with you. It does not post, schedule or click for you.

blocks.text: Many marketers do not have a content shortage. They have a reuse problem. A long article takes days to plan, write and edit, then the social side gets a rushed post and a few lines copied from the summary. The rest of the piece sits in a folder nobody opens again. This page explains why that happens, what it costs, and how to fix it with a routine you can run on a Mac.
Why turning one long piece into many posts stalls

Repurposing shows up on a lot of marketers' lists. In CMI's 2025 B2B benchmark report, 37% of B2B marketers named content repurposing as a challenge. That survey had 980 B2B respondents, and fieldwork ran in summer 2024. Repurposing was a new answer option that year, so there is no earlier number to compare against.

The bigger pressure sits underneath. CMI's 2026 report, based on fieldwork in summer 2025, says 39% of B2B marketers name resource constraints among their top three content challenges. Resource constraints means time, people and budget. Reuse work has no deadline of its own, so it slips first when those run short.
What it costs you in hours and money

The best time figure I could source comes from Sprout Social. Its Social Media Productivity Report, as summarized on Sprout's site, says full-time social marketers spend about 5 hours a week on content creation and approvals. That figure bundles creation with approvals, and the page lists no sample size. Read it as the scale of the work, not the cost of repurposing alone.

Put a price on the time with care. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a 2025 median of $79.70 an hour for advertising, promotions and marketing managers. Five hours a week at that rate comes to about $20,700 a year. That is my estimate from a manager median, not a measured cost of repurposing, and your own rate will differ.

blocks.title: Use your own numbers
blocks.text: Replace the hourly rate and the weekly hours with your own. A coordinator and a director will get very different totals from the same routine, so the math is only a starting point.

Tools add a second cost. Buffer's pricing page lists Essentials at $5 a month per channel and Team at $10 a month per channel. Its free plan covers 3 channels with 10 scheduled posts per channel. Some annual figures on the same page do not match, so check the pricing page at checkout before you commit.
Repurposing is not crossposting

Buffer's repurposing guide says: Repurposing isn't crossposting. Make modifications to fit the platform. Its LinkedIn example uses snappier language and a more skimmable structure. That means every post carries a rewrite cost, even when the idea is already written. Budget for that rewrite, or the routine will quietly stop.

blocks.text: Why it keeps going wrong

items: The plan starts after the article is already published.
Every platform gets the same text with a new link.
The long piece has no clear hook for short formats.
Approvals turn each post into a small meeting.
Nobody owns the queue once the article is live.

blocks.text: Buffer's guide names the core issue. It says practicing repurposing content regularly is the struggle, and that repurposing doesn't become a part of workflows so easily. Its fix is to plan repurposing during content creation, not afterward. I agree, and that is the first fix below.

Writing tools may cut the rewrite time, but the evidence is thin. A Science study by Noy and Zhang, published in 2023, gave 453 college-educated professionals writing tasks. With ChatGPT, average time dropped by 40% and output quality rose by 18%. The tasks were short and generic. The study did not test social repurposing, and I could only read a blog summary of it, not the paper.

blocks.title: Do not publish the first draft
blocks.text: A rewrite tool gives you a starting point. Read every post against the article, check every number and link, and fix the tone before anything goes live.
Fixes you can use today without buying anything
Most of these fixes use apps you already have. Only the video step asks you to try a tool with its own plan. Start with the first fix, since the rest depend on it.
Plan the posts before you write the article

Make a post map at the bottom of the long draft. In Google Docs, choose Insert > Table, and give the grid one row per post. Columns can be idea, platform, link and status. Write the map while the article is still fresh, when you already know which lines matter most.
Track status in a Google Sheet

The doc holds what each post says. A Google Sheet holds where each post stands. Keep the same four columns in the sheet: idea, platform, status and publish date. When you batch, filter the status column to see only drafts that still need work. The filter steps are in [how to add a filter in Google Sheets](/how-to/add-a-filter-to-a-range-in-google-sheets).
Rewrite with a per-platform checklist

items: Open with the point, not the setup.
Keep one example from the article and cut the rest.
Read the post aloud once, then trim anything you stumble over.
End with one question or one clear next step.
Check that every link and number matches the source.

blocks.text: Use Writing Tools for the rough pass

Select a paragraph, then use Writing Tools to rewrite it in the Concise or Friendly tone. Proofread runs a grammar and clarity pass. Key Points pulls the main claims into a short list you can turn into posts. Apple says Writing Tools work in most places you write, including third-party apps and websites. Apple Intelligence on Mac needs macOS 27 and an M1 chip or later.
Turn video into clips only when the source fits

Descript's Create clips feature can make 1 to 20 clips, each 10 seconds to 5 minutes long, with optional 9:16 or 1:1 layouts. Its help pages say the source must be at least as long as the clips you want. Compositions under 1 minute may not generate clips at all. The feature uses AI Credits on current plans, and the help page gives no credit amounts. After clips exist, Canva's Resize feature can move one design into the frame each platform expects.
Batch approvals and scheduling

Post the week's drafts into one Slack thread per post, with the article link and the platform in the first line. Approvals go faster when the reviewer sees the source next to the draft. Schedule only approved posts. Buffer's pricing page does not mention a Mac desktop app, but it does list a Raycast integration that adds posts from the menu bar.
A worked example: one webinar recording

Say you recorded a webinar about onboarding emails. The recording runs long, and the transcript holds many ideas. Your goal is not a post for every minute of video. Your goal is a set of posts where each one makes a single point, works on its own, and points back to the full recording.

Start with the transcript. Mark the moments where the speaker makes a claim, shares a result or answers a hard question. Those moments usually hold up better than the summary slides. Put each one in the post map with its timestamp. Write the LinkedIn post first, since its structure is the easiest to check. Make the short clip last, once you know which moment still makes sense without context.
Mistakes people make when they repurpose content

items: Crossposting the same text everywhere and calling it done.
Choosing the post topics before reading the article again.
Skipping the hook, so the first line says what the article is about.
Letting a rewrite tool write the final version.
Dropping the source link, so readers cannot check the claim.
Starting a video clip from a source that is too short.

blocks.text: Some material does not repurpose well. A dense research report may not split into short clips at all. A product update may need one announcement post and nothing more. When an article holds one strong idea, one good post can be enough. Forcing a full set from thin material wastes the week.

blocks.text: Apple's Shortcuts guide says each shortcut is a series of actions. Build one that takes your highlighted text, adds the platform name and the date, and copies the result. Then run it from the Services menu. You do not need to write code. Test it on one post before you rely on it.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Use it while you work the routine. Keep the article open, hold ⌥⌘, and ask which paragraphs could stand alone as a post. Ask it to draft a LinkedIn version of one paragraph in plain language. Lazur drafts and types text. You still check the facts, the tone and every link before anything goes out.

Dictation helps when the idea arrives before the draft. Hold fn and speak into the cursor in any app. Dictation is unlimited on both Pro and Power, and it works in the post map or the Slack thread. Lazur does not post, schedule or click anything for you, so the publishing step stays yours.

Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report. Use it to see how brands in your niche split one webinar or article into posts. Then check their sources yourself, since a summary can miss a detail.
Pricing and privacy before you try Lazur

Lazur Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 250 AI actions. Power is $120 a month, or $96 a month billed annually, with 1,000 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both. There is a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Check the [pricing page](/pricing) for current terms.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. If your article includes client data, patient data or unreleased plans, follow your employer's rules before you paste it into any tool.
Start this week with one article

Pick one article you already published. Give it a post map, a sheet row for each idea, and one rewrite today. Do the second rewrite tomorrow. Do not build the whole system first. A routine that runs once a week beats a plan that stays in a folder. You can get the app from the [download page](/download).

faq.question: How many social posts should one long article make?
faq.answer: There is no fixed count. Make one post for each standalone idea that fits a platform. A thin article may give you one good post. Forcing a full set from weak material wastes time and reads like filler.

faq.question: Can I copy one post to every platform?
faq.answer: That is crossposting. Buffer's repurposing guide says repurposing isn't crossposting and that you should make modifications to fit the platform. Keep the same claim, then rewrite the wording and structure.

faq.question: Does Apple Writing Tools work on my Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's requirements page lists macOS 27 and Mac with M1 or later. Your device language and Siri language must match, and usage limits may apply. Older Macs cannot use these features.

faq.question: Can Lazur post or schedule for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points, guides, explains, drafts and types text. You post and schedule in the apps you already use.

faq.question: What about turning a recording into clips?
faq.answer: Descript's Create clips can make 1 to 20 clips, each 10 seconds to 5 minutes long. The source must be at least as long as the clips you want. Compositions under 1 minute may not generate clips, and the feature uses AI Credits.

faq.question: How much does Lazur cost, and is there a trial?
faq.answer: There is a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card, and it starts when you first open the app. Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 250 AI actions. Power is $120 a month, or $96 a month billed annually, with 1,000 AI actions.

faq.question: Does Buffer have a Mac app?
faq.answer: Buffer's pricing page does not mention a Mac desktop app. It does list a Raycast integration that lets you create and schedule Buffer posts from your Mac menu bar. Check their pricing page before you sign up.

faq.question: Is my content used to train AI?
faq.answer: Lazur says content is never used to train AI models. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. If your content includes client or patient data, follow your employer's rules first.

costs.title: Hours that disappear into creation and approval
costs.text: Sprout Social reports full-time social marketers spend about 5 hours a week on content creation and approvals. Repurposing is part of that work, but the figure does not isolate it. Count your own week before you decide what the routine costs you.

costs.title: A rewrite on every platform
costs.text: Buffer's guide says repurposing isn't crossposting, and each platform needs changes. Each post carries its own rewrite, even when the idea is already written. That rewrite is the step that takes real attention.

costs.title: Visual work that does not come easily
costs.text: Buffer's guide says creating visual assets from written content isn't as easy as repurposing into another text-friendly format. Not every written piece can be distilled into a 15 to 60 second clip. Plan for a slower visual step, or skip it for pieces that do not fit.

costs.title: Tool spend that adds up
costs.text: Buffer's pricing page lists Essentials at $5 a month per channel and Team at $10 a month per channel. Descript's help page says Create clips uses AI Credits, without giving amounts. Add up the channels and the credits before you pick a stack.

costs.title: Good lines that never get published
costs.text: When repurposing does not become part of the workflow, the article's best lines stay in the draft. Buffer's guide names practicing repurposing regularly as the struggle. The cost is reach you never got, and you cannot measure that from the draft alone.

costs.title: Pay for the hours at your own rate
costs.text: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a 2025 median of $79.70 an hour for advertising, promotions and marketing managers. Five hours a week at that rate is about $20,700 a year. Treat this as an estimate. Your own hourly cost is the number to use.

causes.title: The plan starts too late
causes.text: Buffer's guidance is to plan repurposing during content creation. When the plan starts after publishing, the article is finished and the energy is gone. Nobody wants to reread a long piece just to find the posts inside it.

causes.title: Each platform needs its own voice
causes.text: Buffer says repurposing isn't crossposting. A LinkedIn reader wants a structured point. A short video viewer wants a hook. When one text goes everywhere, it fits none of them well.

causes.title: Not every piece has a clear clip
causes.text: Buffer's guide says not every written piece can be distilled into a short 15 to 60 second clip. Long pieces often hold argument and context, and context does not fit into short formats. Pick the moments that stand alone.

causes.title: Approvals stretch the work
causes.text: Sprout Social's 5 hour figure bundles creation with approvals. Each approval round adds delay to every post in the set, so approvals are part of the real cost. Batch the reviews to reduce the drag.

causes.title: Limited people and budget
causes.text: CMI's 2026 report says 39% of B2B marketers name resource constraints among their top three content challenges. Time, people and budget make up that category. Repurposing has no fixed deadline, so it loses to the next launch.

causes.title: Writing takes longer than it should
causes.text: The Noy and Zhang study found a 40% drop in time on short generic writing tasks with ChatGPT access. That suggests drafting help can reduce the rewrite load. The study did not test social repurposing, so treat that as a hint, not a result.

fixes.title: Plan the post map before the article ships
fixes.text: Write one line per post in a Google Docs table while the draft is open. Each line names the idea, the platform and the link. If you cannot name the platform, the idea is not ready to post.

fixes.title: Keep the plan in Docs and the status in Sheets
fixes.text: The doc holds what each post says. A Google Sheet holds where each post stands. Splitting the two keeps the doc readable and gives you a filter for the week's drafts.

fixes.title: Use a per-platform checklist
fixes.text: Open with the point, keep one example, end with one question or next step, and check each number against the source. The checklist removes the guesswork that makes repurposing slow. Use the same checklist every week so it becomes habit.

fixes.title: Use Writing Tools for the rough pass only
fixes.text: Use Writing Tools to rewrite, proofread or pull key points from a paragraph. Read every output against the article before you keep it. Apple requires macOS 27 and an M1 chip or later, so older Macs will not get these features.

fixes.title: Clip video only when the source is long enough
fixes.text: Check that the source is at least as long as the clip you want. Skip compositions under 1 minute, since they may not generate clips. Check the AI Credit use in Descript before you run a large batch.

fixes.title: Batch approvals in one Slack thread
fixes.text: Post the week's drafts together, with one thread per post. Put the article link and the platform first. Approve in one pass, then schedule only what passed.

fixes.title: Use Shortcuts for the repeat steps
fixes.text: Build a shortcut for the parts you repeat, such as adding the date and platform to a draft. Shortcuts can run from the Services menu or a keyboard shortcut, so the routine takes fewer clicks.

fixes.title: Pick a scheduler that matches your channels
fixes.text: Buffer's free plan allows 3 channels and 10 scheduled posts per channel. If you need more, compare the paid rate per channel on the pricing page before you move up a plan.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pick one article and list its ideas
plan.text: Open the long piece. Highlight every point that could stand alone. Paste each idea into a Google Sheet row with a platform and a status column. Stop at the ideas, not the posts.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Build the post map
plan.text: Write one line per post in a Google Docs table. Name the platform on each line. Add the article link once, at the top of the table, so every post points back to it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Rewrite for each platform
plan.text: Draft each post in the voice of its platform. Use the checklist: open with the point, keep one example, end with one question or next step. Proofread last, against the source.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Make the visuals
plan.text: Resize one Canva design for each format you use. For video, check that the source is longer than the clip you want, then make clips only if the source fits.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Approve and schedule
plan.text: Post the batch to one Slack thread for approval. Schedule only the approved posts in your scheduler. Set a reminder for next week's review before you close the laptop.
